name: Notion
thesis: Notion gives one person everything free and charges when a second person joins, and its template gallery manufactures those first people at search scale. Whether it wins new users or re-engages old ones, Notion has never said.

sections.title: Vitals
sections.summary: A company that publishes a valuation and no user count, not even on its own About page.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.summary: Described by its users, not by the company: too rigid for Jira, too loose for a wiki.

sections.title: Users & Segments
sections.summary: The pricing page names four audiences. The gallery says the biggest one is students.

sections.title: Jobs To Be Done
sections.summary: Two jobs, both quoted from the January 2019 launch thread.

sections.title: The Product
sections.summary: One primitive, the block. It is also the thing you are billed against.

sections.title: Business Model
sections.summary: A cap that counts what you ever created, not what you still keep.

sections.title: Growth Loops
sections.summary: Four links evidenced, one missing, and the missing one is the whole question.

sections.title: Moats
sections.summary: Getting in is a click. Getting out is the thing people have complained about since 2019.

sections.title: Bets & Tensions
sections.summary: AI is now a plan gate and, by Notion's careful wording, more than half of something.

sections.title: Verdict
sections.summary: Our call, with the ceiling stated.

problem.beforeState: By the account of users at its January 2019 launch, teams were choosing between project tools too rigid for how they worked and documents too loose to track anything, running Asana or Jira for tasks and Evernote, OneNote or Google Docs for knowledge, with no way to keep the two in the same place. This is how users described the world before, not how Notion described it.
problem.afterState: One workspace where a note, a task, a table and a wiki page are the same kind of object, so a team can shape its own tool rather than adopt someone else's. Notion's own framing is a mission to break away from today's tools and bring back ideas from early computing pioneers, which is a statement of intent rather than a measured change.
problem.wedge: A single composable primitive, the block, that made a document and a database the same material, sold to the person who wanted to arrange their own workflow.

whyNow.change: By the late 2010s teams ran both a rigid tracker and a loose document tool, and increasingly resented maintaining the seam between them.
whyNow.argument: A user at launch put the position better than any marketing did, calling it the balance between strict project tools and completely unstructured wikis. That names a gap in the market, but the record does not establish whether the gap opened then or had always been there.

segments.name: Individuals and students
segments.description: People organising their own lives, and the largest group by any observable measure: the gallery's biggest categories are Personal Planner, Student Life and Study Planner, not anything to do with work. Free forever for one person, which is why this group is invisible in revenue and dominant in the funnel.

segments.name: Small teams and startups
segments.description: The group the business model is actually aimed at. A second member turns an unlimited workspace into a 1,000-block one, and Notion's own audience line for Plus is small teams and professionals working together. The 2019 accounts of teams dropping Asana and Jira describe this segment forming.

segments.name: Enterprises
segments.description: Organisations buying SSO, SCIM, audit logs, domain management and zero data retention with model providers. Priced on request, and the only tier where Notion names control and security rather than flexibility as the thing being sold.

segments.name: Template creators
segments.description: Over 22,000 people with public creator profiles who build the inventory the gallery ranks on. They are users, suppliers and a distribution channel at once. What any of them earns is not established by anything in the record.

powerUser.profile: Someone who stopped using Notion as a notebook and started using it as a system: linked databases, templates they built themselves, and a workspace other people now depend on. At launch a user described documenting every important procedure simply because it had become enjoyable, and another had already built a site for sharing their pages with strangers.
behaviours: Builds databases with relations rather than writing flat pages
Makes templates for their own repeated work, then publishes some
Replaces two or three separate tools with one workspace
Invites collaborators, which is what triggers the block limit

notFor.who: Teams who want the tool to decide
notFor.why: One team lead described the flexibility of blocks as cognitive overhead and said his team would rather have something constrained like Trello, calling Notion a jack of all trades and master of none after trying it as a wiki, project tracker and issue tracker. One team's experience, and the clearest statement of what the product trades away.

notFor.who: Anyone who needs their content to leave easily
notFor.why: Users have described difficulty getting content out since launch in 2019, and one paying customer reported the export feature silently failing for three months in 2021. Two accounts, not a measured rate.

jobs.statement: When my team needs to track work, give us something we can shape ourselves so we don't have to adopt Jira's process.

competingAlternatives.name: Asana
competingAlternatives.why: The tool one team left, in their words, after getting annoyed with it and not wanting to move to something like Jira.

competingAlternatives.name: Jira
competingAlternatives.why: Named twice in the launch thread: once as the thing being avoided, once as the thing Notion was used in lieu of.

competingAlternatives.name: Trello
competingAlternatives.why: Named by a team lead who went the other way, preferring a constrained tool to Notion's flexibility.

forces.push: A tracker whose process did not match how the team worked, and the overhead of maintaining it alongside separate documents.
forces.pull: Freeform structure, in one team's words letting them create a workflow that fit them, with tasks and the docs about them in one place.
forces.anxiety: That the flexibility becomes its own cost. One team lead called it cognitive overhead and went back to something constrained.
forces.habit: An existing tracker with history in it, and colleagues who already know where things live.

jobs.statement: When I keep notes for myself, let me structure them so I can find things again without guessing the right keyword.

competingAlternatives.name: Evernote
competingAlternatives.why: The tool most often named as replaced, by users who said they had not looked back.

competingAlternatives.name: OneNote
competingAlternatives.why: One user described drafting emails into an unorganised OneNote notebook and having to search and hope they remembered the keyword.

competingAlternatives.name: Google Docs
competingAlternatives.why: Named by a user who found Notion easier to navigate and structure, because it removed the file and folder distinction.

forces.push: Notes that accumulate faster than they can be organised, and retrieval that depends on remembering the right words.
forces.pull: Nesting, linking and embedding pages inside pages, so structure emerges instead of being filed.
forces.anxiety: Porting years of existing notes in, which one user said they could not imagine doing, and the difficulty of getting content out later.
forces.habit: A decade of notes already living somewhere else.

coreActions: Add a block, which is any piece of content
Nest blocks inside blocks to build a page
Turn a set of pages into a database with views
Duplicate a template into a workspace
Publish a page to the web
Submit a template to the gallery
Edit the same page as someone else, merged rather than overwritten
product.atomicUnitOfValue: A block: the smallest thing you can create, the thing pages are made of, and the thing the free plan counts.

keySurfaces.name: The editor
keySurfaces.purpose: Where blocks are written and nested, with concurrent edits merged by a CRDT since July 2025. Not observed here; it requires an account.

keySurfaces.name: Databases
keySurfaces.purpose: Collections of pages with properties and views: table, board, calendar, gallery.

keySurfaces.name: Template gallery
keySurfaces.purpose: Public, unauthenticated catalogue of 30,000+ templates organised into 348 categories.

keySurfaces.name: Notion Sites
keySurfaces.purpose: Publishes any page to the open web, which is how template artefacts are distributed and read by people with no account.

keySurfaces.name: Notion AI
keySurfaces.purpose: Agents and assistance, gated to Business and Enterprise, with premium models metered by credits.

keySurfaces.name: API
keySurfaces.purpose: Reads and writes blocks, with 30+ block types and nesting, arriving in 2021 after two years of requests.

businessModel.valueMetric: The member. Price is per person per month, and the free plan's block cap is triggered not by volume but by adding a second one.

revenueLines.name: Per-member subscriptions
revenueLines.description: Plus at $10 and Business at $20 per member per month, with Enterprise on request. Independent reporting puts total ARR recently past $600 million and the company cash flow positive; Notion discloses no split, so this line carries everything.

revenueLines.name: AI, sold as a tier and metered above it
revenueLines.description: AI is not an add-on. It is the main reason to be on Business rather than Plus, with premium models spending credits on top. Notion says more than half of ARR now comes from customers who use AI, which is a statement about customers rather than about AI revenue.

tiers.name: Free
gates: Unlimited for one person; 1,000 blocks once a second member joins
5 MB file uploads, 10 guests, 7 days of page history
A limited number of complimentary AI responses

tiers.name: Plus
gates: Unlimited guests, 30 days of page history
tiers.priceNote: $10 per member per month, as of 2026-09-22

tiers.name: Business
gates: Notion AI, agents, meeting notes and enterprise search
SAML SSO and granular database permissions
tiers.priceNote: $20 per member per month, marked Recommended

tiers.name: Enterprise
gates: Zero data retention with model providers
SCIM provisioning, audit log, domain management

businessModel.monetizationMoment: Inviting the second person. A workspace with one member has no block limit; a workspace with two is capped at 1,000 blocks, counted from everything ever created and never reduced by deleting. Collaboration is the trigger, not volume.
businessModel.unitEconomicsShape: Free for individuals at unlimited scale, which is unusual and is what fills the gallery with 22,000 creators making inventory. The cap lands precisely where collaboration begins, so the cost of the free tier is borne against personal users while the conversion pressure sits on teams. Reported ARR passed $600 million with the company cash flow positive, on figures nobody has audited.

brief.grows: Someone searches for a planner, lands on a template page, sees the whole working thing without an account, and has to sign up to keep it. Some later publish templates of their own.
brief.earns: Per member: free and unlimited for one person, a 1,000-block lifetime cap once a second member joins, then $10 or $20 a seat, with AI reserved for the $20 plan.
brief.tradeoff: In 2020 it dropped its $4 personal plan to make individuals free forever, trading revenue for the population that now fills the template gallery.
brief.unverified: How many of the 11 million people who duplicated templates in a year were new to Notion.

verdict.thesis: Notion gives one person everything free and charges when a second person joins, and its template gallery manufactures those first people at search scale. Whether it wins new users or re-engages old ones, Notion has never said.

getRight.argument: One person has no limit; a second member caps the workspace at 1,000 blocks. The paywall lands at collaboration, where the product is worth most and a team budget usually exists.

getRight.claim: The product is its own landing page
getRight.argument: A template page renders the whole working artefact to someone with no account, and the signup arrives only when they want to keep it. The value is shown before the ask.

getRight.claim: It productised something users already did
getRight.argument: Users were building sites to share Notion pages in 2019, four years before the gallery relaunch. The gallery then grew from 600 templates to over 30,000 by following that behaviour rather than inventing it.

getWrong.claim: Getting content out has been hard since launch
getWrong.argument: A user said so at the 2019 launch, and in 2021 a paying customer's export failed for three months while support cited a backlog. The oldest complaint about the product is still its only evidenced moat.

getWrong.claim: An AI metric nobody can falsify
getWrong.argument: More than half of ARR from AI-enabled customers counts every dollar from any customer who touches AI. Bundling AI into the $20 plan means AI revenue cannot be separated, so the headline cannot be tested.

getWrong.claim: A cap that punishes tidying up
getWrong.argument: Deleting blocks never restores capacity, because the cap counts everything ever created. Users have described it as arbitrary since at least 2020.

whatIdDoNext.rationale: Tag each duplication by whether the account was created in that session, and report it. It is one field in a query Notion already runs, and it would settle whether the gallery acquires or re-engages.
whatIdDoNext.risk: If most duplicators already had accounts, the gallery looks like a retention feature and loses its place in the growth story.

whatIdDoNext.move: Count stored blocks, not created ones
whatIdDoNext.rationale: Let deletion free capacity on the free team cap. The trigger for paying should be collaboration, which it already is, not a penalty for tidying.
whatIdDoNext.risk: Some teams will manage their way under the cap indefinitely and convert later, or never.

whatIdDoNext.move: Make export a feature, not a support ticket
whatIdDoNext.rationale: A reliable export that keeps databases and structure would turn the oldest complaint into a trust signal for enterprise buyers, who check exit costs before they sign.
whatIdDoNext.risk: It lowers the switching cost that is currently Notion's only evidenced moat.

openQuestions: What share of template duplicators were new to Notion?
Do people who duplicate a template come back a week later?
What does a template creator earn, and what share earn anything?
What did Skiff, Flowdash, Cron, Automate.io and ZeroEntropy cost?
How much of Notion's ARR is earned by AI, as opposed to paid by customers who use it?

interview.question: Notion's free plan is unlimited for one person. Why is that a good business decision?
outline: Dropping the $4 personal plan in 2020 traded revenue for population
Those individuals build and publish templates, which is the supply side of the gallery
The cap lands at the second member, where value concentrates and a budget usually exists
The cost is serving an unbounded free population, which forced a large sharding effort

interview.question: Is Notion's template gallery an acquisition channel? How would you prove it?
outline: Map the chain: search, template page, the artefact itself, the signup wall, duplication
Say what is evidenced: traffic estimates, 51 million duplications, and the documented wall
Name the missing metric: the share of duplications made by accounts created in that session
Design the test: flag new accounts at duplication and compare their retention to existing users

interview.question: More than half of Notion's ARR comes from AI-enabled customers. What would you ask before believing AI is working?
outline: Separate a customer share from a revenue share
Bundling AI into the $20 plan makes AI revenue impossible to separate by construction
Ask for AI-attributable effects: upgrades driven by AI, usage per seat, retention with and without it
Check the margin: inference cost against a flat per-seat price

interview.question: What would you change about the 1,000-block cap?
outline: State what it counts: blocks ever created, not blocks stored
State what triggers it: a second member joining
Note the user reaction: described as arbitrary since at least 2020
Offer options: count stored blocks, a soft cap, or block credits for publishing templates
Name the trade-off: every option weakens the conversion pressure on teams

patterns.note: One member is unlimited; a second member caps the workspace at 1,000 lifetime blocks.
Template pages render the full working artefact to anonymous visitors, and keeping it requires an account.
Duplicating a template in is one click; getting structure out has drawn complaints since 2019.
